title: Emotions and Decision-Making
keyIdea: Feelings change the choices we make. When a feeling is very strong, like fury or panic, we notice fewer options and grab the fastest one, such as a mean reply. When we are calm, more options come back. Strong feelings fade with time, so pausing before a big choice gives you more control. Feelings are still useful clues: fear can warn of real danger, so notice them, then decide.

kid: Feelings steer your choices. If a friend posts a joke about you and you feel furious, you may only see two moves: hit back or storm off. When you are calm, you can see more. You could ask what they meant, laugh it off or talk tomorrow.
The same moment looks different hot and cool. In a hot moment you might shout or slam a door. With a cool head you might say, That made me really cross, and fix the problem.
Big feelings fade if you give them time. An angry text that feels right now can look harsh in twenty minutes. So pause before you send, post or decide. Breathe, walk away or sleep on it.

Feelings are not the enemy. Fear when a stranger asks you to get in a car is a warning, so listen to it. Anger or disappointment about a small thing needs cooling first. Notice, pause, list options, think what happens next, then choose.
adult: This topic is for ages 9 to 11. Children learn that emotions shape thinking and choices. Strong feelings can cloud judgement. We often choose differently when calm than when upset. Seeing this gives us more control.

Research backs the simple story. Strong negative emotions narrow attention to a few fast, defensive actions, while calm states widen the options we consider. Acute stress also weakens the planning functions of the brain for a while. Arousal falls with time, which is why a cooling-off pause works. Emotions also carry useful signals: fear and unease often flag real risk.

Common mistakes: thinking feelings should be ignored or bottled up, believing a choice made at the peak of anger is the true one, assuming the situation changed when only the feeling did, and labelling a child as bad for being angry. Be careful not to teach that all feelings are bad for decisions. Teach the pause, not the suppression.

In the lab your child turns an anger dial up and watches four of six choices vanish. They sort hot and cool choices, then wait out an angry text before rewriting and sending it. They build a five-step stop-think-choose plan and decide when a feeling is a warning and when it needs cooling.

familyTip: When everyone is calm, agree a family pause signal, like a time-out hand sign, that anyone can use in an argument. Afterwards, talk through one recent choice: What did you feel? What did you do? What might you choose with a cool head?

practice.prompt: Sam is furious after losing a game. He can only think of throwing the controller. Why?
choices: Strong anger narrows the choices he notices
Throwing it is the only choice there is
He is a bad person
practice.hint: Think about the anger dial. What happened to the choices as it went up?
practice.explain: Strong feelings narrow attention. Sam could also take a break or shake hands, but fury hides those options.

practice.prompt: Mia writes an angry text and waits {n} minutes before sending. What is most likely?
choices: She feels calmer and changes the words
She feels angrier and sends it twice
Nothing about her feeling changes
practice.hint: What happens to strong feelings when you give them time?
practice.explain: Strong feelings fade with time. After {n} minutes, Mia is likely to see that the text is too harsh and rewrite it.

practice.prompt: Your brother breaks your model. Which is a cool-head choice?
choices: Say "That made me really cross" and ask him to help fix it
Break one of his toys back
Slam the door and shout
practice.hint: Which choice names the feeling and fixes the problem?
practice.explain: Naming the feeling and fixing the problem are cool-head choices. Getting even and slamming doors come from a hot moment.

practice.prompt: Which step comes first in the stop-think-choose plan?
choices: Notice the feeling
Choose what to do
Think what happens next
practice.hint: You cannot cool a feeling you have not spotted.
practice.explain: First notice the feeling, then pause, list options, think what happens next, and choose last.

practice.prompt: At {n} metres up a climbing frame, Leo feels scared that a bar is loose. Should he ignore the fear?
choices: No, it may be a real warning, so he should check or climb down
Yes, feelings always get in the way
Yes, to prove he is brave
practice.hint: Can fear ever be a useful clue?
practice.explain: Fear can warn of real danger. At {n} metres a loose bar matters, so Leo should listen, climb down and tell an adult.

pool.prompt: How do strong feelings affect decisions?
choices: They can cloud judgement and push fast choices
They always make decisions better
They have no effect at all
pool.hint: Think of the angry text you nearly sent.
pool.explain: Strong feelings can cloud judgement. We grab the fastest choice and may regret it later.

choices: Pausing until a strong feeling fades before you decide
Never feeling anything
Deciding as fast as you can
pool.hint: Think of waiting before you press send.
pool.explain: Cooling off is pausing, by breathing, walking away or waiting, until the feeling drops and you can think clearly.

pool.prompt: Zoe quits the team {n} minutes after losing. The next day she regrets it. What happened?
choices: Disappointment rushed a big decision
She made the right choice; feelings never change
She is just a quitter
pool.hint: Was she calm when she decided?
pool.explain: Only {n} minutes after losing, Zoe was still upset. The feeling rushed a big decision that looked different the next day.

pool.prompt: The same message from a friend looks rude when you are upset and fine when you are calm. Why?
choices: Your feeling changes how you read it
The friend changed the words
Your feelings were wrong to have
pool.hint: Did the message change, or did you?
pool.explain: The words stayed the same. Being upset makes things look worse; calm lets you read them fairly.

pool.prompt: Which feeling is a warning you should listen to?
choices: Feeling scared when a stranger asks you to get in their car
Feeling furious when someone pushes in the queue
Feeling like quitting after one bad game
pool.hint: Which one protects you from danger?
pool.explain: Fear around a stranger's car is a safety warning. The others are feelings to cool before you act.

pool.prompt: Ava has a big argument and takes {n} slow breaths before she replies. Why does this help?
choices: It turns the feeling down so she can think of more options
It makes her forget the argument
It proves she was wrong
pool.hint: What happened to the choices as the anger dial went down?
pool.explain: Pausing for {n} slow breaths lowers the feeling, so more options come back into view.

pool.prompt: Which is the full stop-think-choose order?
choices: Notice, pause, list options, think ahead, choose
Choose, then think later
List options, choose, then notice the feeling
pool.hint: Start by noticing the feeling. Choosing comes last.
pool.explain: Notice the feeling, pause, list options, think what each leads to, then choose.

pool.prompt: What is the best thing to do with a strong feeling?
choices: Notice and name it, then pause before acting
Bottle it up and pretend it is not there
Act on it straight away
pool.hint: Feelings are not wrong to have.
pool.explain: Noticing and naming a feeling, then pausing, gives you control. Bottling it up or acting at once does not.

visual.caption: Which choice comes from a hot moment, and which from a cool head? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: turn up the anger dial, sort hot and cool choices, wait out an angry text, build the stop-think-choose plan, know when to listen to a feeling.
